analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a Senate vote: it sat in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee after a July 1991 hearing until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the Interior Department from any oil and gas leasing, exploration, or drilling on the outer continental shelf off Florida — the waters south of 26° north latitude and within 100 nautical miles of Florida's coast [S3]. It would also cancel every existing federal lease in those waters and pay the leaseholders whatever compensation the law entitles them to, with Florida bearing none of the cost [S3]. In a separate band of the Eastern Gulf off Florida's west coast, it would block all drilling activity until at least 2002, while the Interior Department completes environmental studies reviewed by independent scientists [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held a hearing in July 1991 but never sent it to the floor [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal communities, tourism and fishing businesses, and everyone who uses the state's beaches and waters would gain protection from offshore drilling, spills, and onshore oil infrastructure. The state itself would be shielded from any liability for canceling the leases [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida's coast, beaches, and tourism economy

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits the Secretary of the Interior from any leasing or drilling activity under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act in the waters south of 26° north latitude and east of 86° west longitude, and within 100 nautical miles of Florida's coastline [S3].
It requires cancellation of all existing leases in those areas and makes Florida incur no cost or liability for the cancellations, with compensation paid from the U.S. Treasury [S3].

In the Eastern Gulf of Mexico Planning Area off Florida's western boundary, it bans lease sales, exploration plans, development plans, drilling permits, and drilling itself until at least January 1, 2002, and until required environmental studies — reviewed by independent scientists nominated by the Florida Academy of Sciences — are complete [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies would lose existing leases (compensated with federal dollars) and lose access to a large area of federal waters. Taxpayers would fund the compensation payments and up to $1 million per year for ten years of environmental studies [S3]. Energy consumers forgo whatever oil and gas might have been produced there, though any production in this particular area was far off in the future.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill cancels existing leases and pays lessees compensation out of the U.S. Treasury, so taxpayers bear the cost of buying back drilling rights the government already sold [S3].
The bill authorizes $1 million per year for fiscal years 1992 through 2001 for environmental studies, a recurring federal expense [S3].
By permanently closing an area to leasing, the bill forgoes domestic energy production and the federal revenue that offshore leases and royalties would have generated [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida, the trade was strongly one-sided: the state's beach- and tourism-driven economy, fishing industry, and coastal environment were protected from drilling risk, while the direct costs — lease compensation and study funding — fell on the federal Treasury. The main honest objection is the permanent closure of a large area to domestic energy production and the taxpayer-funded buyback of existing leases; but there was no active drilling in most of the closed area, so the near-term energy cost was small.

outcome.mechanism: It died in committee: the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee referred the bill, took comment from Interior and the budget office, held a hearing in July 1991, and never reported it out before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill on March 21, 1991, joined by Sen. Connie Mack, Florida's two senators from opposite parties, and it drew 9 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 2 Republicans) [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day it was introduced; it never left that committee [S5].

The committee requested executive comment from the Department of the Interior and the Office of Management and Budget in June 1991 and held a hearing on July 17, 1991 (printed as S.Hrg. 102-224) [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a Senate vote and expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding offshore leases off Florida kept them without cancellation, and the oil and gas industry kept the closed areas available for future leasing; the Interior Department kept discretion over the Eastern Gulf.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore leaseholders and the oil and gas industry

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently bar drilling off Florida's coasts and cancel existing leases.

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack

for.what_they_did: Joined Graham in introducing the bill.

for.name: 2 of 100 Senate Republicans and 7 of 56 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from the Florida delegation and beyond.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its July 1991 hearing; it was never reported to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Department of the Interior

against.what_they_did: Was asked for executive comment on the bill in June 1991; the Department's leasing program was the target of the bill's prohibitions.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Florida's two senators, a Democrat and a Republican, introduced it together, with cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and there is no record of a party-line vote because the bill never reached the floor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would permanently close waters off Florida to leasing, exploration, and drilling, and cancel existing leases with federal compensation [S3]. Drilling there would put spill risk on Florida's beaches and fishing grounds, so the industry's interest ran against the state's coastal economy.
Protecting the coast from drilling activity protects the beaches, waters, and fisheries that Florida's tourism and fishing businesses depend on; their interest ran alongside the public's [S3].
